title: Microanalysis of Natural Materials Subjected to the Space Environment
content: The conditions at the surface of the Moon are extreme and lead to the formation of micro- to nanoscale features that are unique compared to natural materials on Earth. There is no atmosphere to speak of on the Moon, and surface pressures are on the order of 10-12 Torr. Equatorial regions experience a diurnal temperature swing of more than 300K, while polar, permanently shadowed regions can be as cold as ∼25K. In addition, the Moon has no planetary-scale magnetic field, and during the lunar day, materials at the lunar surface are almost constantly exposed to UV radiation and the solar wind, which is a plasma of energetic charged particles at low energies (∼1-100 keV/nucleon) [1]. The ions in the solar wind are primarily hydrogen (∼96%) and helium (∼4%) with energies of 1 keV and 4 keV, respectively, but heavy, multiply charged ions are also part of the solar wind. Solar energetic particle (SEP) events can significantly increase the energy of the impacting ions, with energies up to ∼100 MeV/nucleon [2]. Galactic and extra-galactic cosmic rays, while much lower flux, but are notable for their extreme energies from 1 to over 1000 GeV/nucleon [1]. The effects of this irradiation include chemical and structural changes due to implantation, sputtering, and displacement of atoms in the target material, which on the Moon is generally a silicate mineral (plagioclase, olivine, or pyroxene) or the Fe-Ti-oxide ilmenite. Finally, the lack of atmosphere means that the lunar surface is subjected to hypervelocity impacts from sub-millimeter particles known as micrometeoroids with a mass flux of 1.4 tons per day and speeds >20 km/s [3], with slower (<5 km/s), secondary impacts still able to shock, melt, and vaporize material.
